cur:legends-mandylion-vatican.summary: The face of Christ, long-haired and bearded, looks out through a gold cover whose cut-out follows the outline of his head and pointed beard — the traditional form of the Mandylion, the miraculous image sent to King Abgar of Edessa. For centuries it belonged to the Poor Clares of San Silvestro in Capite in Rome, who venerated it as the Edessa image; since 1870 it has been kept in the Vatican. Because it is painted on a wooden panel, scholars regard it as a copy rather than the cloth of the legend.
facts: The earliest record of it dates from 1517, when the nuns of San Silvestro were forbidden to exhibit it, to avoid rivalry with the Veronica at St Peter's.
Its Baroque frame was given in 1623 by Sister Dionora Chiarucci, abbess of the convent.
It was exhibited in the pavilion of the Holy See at Expo 2000 in Hanover, where this photograph was taken.

cur:legends-mandylion-vatican.notes: No technical or art-historical date for the painting could be verified; y=1500 is a placeholder just before the first documentary mention (1517). Photograph by Wolfgang M. (Commons user Bonebendz), GFDL relicensed CC BY-SA 3.0.

cur:manuscripts-trier-apocalypse-sardis.summary: A bust of Christ with a cross-staff appears in a cloud-flecked sky at the upper left; below, John stands with a scroll, and an angel stands among the buildings of Sardis while a small group of figures gather and point.
facts: The Trier Apocalypse contains 74 full-page drawings illustrating about 150 episodes of the Book of Revelation; it is one of the earliest illustrated Apocalypse manuscripts to survive.
Its pictures are thought to copy a late antique model of the 4th–6th century, which explains features such as books shown as scrolls and Christ as the beardless Logos.
cur:manuscripts-trier-apocalypse-sardis.notes: The Commons description assigns this page to the letter to Sardis; the exact letter illustrated is not certain.

cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-28-christ.summary: At the upper left the cross-nimbed Christ-Logos holding a book sits in a globe-mandorla among angels, and personified winds below him breathe out rays, the 'voice of the Lord' that is upon the waters, breaks the cedars of Lebanon and shakes the wilderness. On the right a procession of young men brings lambs to the sanctuary. The drawing gives visible form to a psalm about the sound of God's power.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
Its text is written in rustic capitals, an archaic script that once led scholars to date the manuscript to the 6th century; the drawings are now recognised as Carolingian.
cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-28-christ.notes: The figure of the Lord is identified as Christ (the Christ-Logos) following the commentary of the Utrecht University Library's annotated edition, which describes the psalter's consistent practice of drawing the God of the psalms as the youthful Christ. The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server.

cur:objects2-vam-anglo-saxon-pectoral-cr.summary: On this worn, oval pectoral of walrus ivory the crucified Christ stands calmly before the cross, his feet on a suppedaneum, while the Hand of God descends from a cloud above; four roundels around him hold the symbols of the Evangelists. A hollow cross-shaped cavity at the back once held a relic, so that the wearer carried both the image and the relic of Christ's Passion close to the heart.
facts: The V&A links the figure style and the Hand of God to late Anglo-Saxon stone roods such as those at Stepney and Romsey.
Such pectoral crosses, worn on a chain or cord, were commonly worn by bishops and abbots.
The cross is only 9 cm high.

Q546241.summary: The infant Christ presses his cheek to his mother's and reaches around her neck, while Mary's sorrowful eyes look outward as though foreseeing his Passion. This tender 'Eleousa' (Mercy) type, most likely painted in Constantinople and sent to Kievan Rus', became the most venerated icon in Russia and shaped centuries of Orthodox images of the Christ Child.
facts: It was sent from Constantinople to Kiev around 1131, taken to Vladimir by Prince Andrei Bogolyubsky in 1155, and, according to tradition, brought to Moscow in 1395.
According to tradition, Muscovites credited it with saving the city when Tamerlane's army withdrew in 1395 without attacking.
Only the faces of Mother and Child (and part of the gold ground) belong to the original 12th-century painting; the rest has been restored and overpainted at least five times.
The Child's bare foot, turned so that its sole is visible, is a distinctive detail of this icon, repeated in later copies of the type.

Q318947.summary: At the moment the risen Christ blesses the bread, two disciples recognize him: one grips the arms of his chair as if about to leap up, the other flings his arms wide as if mirroring the Cross. Caravaggio paints a youthful, beardless Christ in a red tunic, lit from the upper left against a dark wall, while the standing innkeeper looks on uncomprehending. The still life on the table, with its bread, roast fowl and fruit basket, makes the sacred encounter almost tangibly present.
facts: The beardless Christ was unusual and surprised early viewers; it may reflect the Gospel of Mark's remark that the risen Jesus appeared 'in another form' (Mark 16:12).
The fruit basket teeters over the table's edge, appearing to project into the viewer's own space — a famous piece of illusionism.

The painting was made for the Roman nobleman Ciriaco Mattei, one of Caravaggio's important early patrons; it soon passed to Cardinal Scipione Borghese and was presented to the National Gallery in 1839.
Caravaggio painted the subject again in 1606 (now in the Pinacoteca di Brera, Milan) in a much more subdued, sombre manner.
